paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Shale is a clastic sedimentary rock with fine grains, and it forms from mud. The mud is a mix of flakes of clay minerals and tiny, silt-sized fragments of other minerals, especially quartz and calcite. Clays are the major constituent. Shale is the most common sedimentary rock.

paragraphs.heading: A rock that splits
paragraphs.text: Shale is marked by its tendency to split into thin layers less than one centimeter thick. This property is called fissility. It comes from the clay mineral flakes, which lie parallel to one another, so the rock breaks into thin layers, often splintery. Rocks of similar composition and particle size that do not split this way are called mudstones or claystones, depending on how much silt they hold. Rocks with similar particle sizes but less clay, more than 2/3 silt, are grittier and are called siltstones.

paragraphs.heading: Ingredients and color
paragraphs.text: Shales are typically grey and made of clay minerals and quartz grains. In a typical shale, clay minerals make up about 58%, quartz 28%, feldspar 6%, carbonate minerals 5% and iron oxides 2%. Varying amounts of minor ingredients change the color. Reds point to hematite, a ferric oxide, and greens to micaceous minerals such as chlorite, biotite and illite. Black shale gets its color from carbonaceous material above one percent, and it is a sign of a reducing environment.

paragraphs.heading: Where it settles
paragraphs.text: The fine particles that make up shale can stay suspended in water long after larger sand particles have been deposited. As a result, shales are typically laid down in very slow moving water. They are often found in lake and lagoon deposits, on floodplains, in river deltas, and offshore beneath the wave base. Most shales are marine in origin.

paragraphs.heading: How clay reaches the bottom
paragraphs.text: Single clay particles settle extremely slowly, so most clay must be deposited as clumps, called aggregates and floccules. This clumping, called flocculation, is very rapid once clay meets highly saline sea water. A single clay particle is under 4 microns in size, while the clumps can be anything between a few tens of microns and more than 700 microns across. The floccules start out rich in water, but over time the clay minerals bind together more tightly and much of that water is expelled.

paragraphs.heading: Organic matter and black shale
paragraphs.text: Of all the organic matter in sedimentary rocks, roughly 95 percent sits in shales and other mudrocks. Even so, that is less than one percent by mass of an average shale. Black shales form in anoxic conditions. Along the margins of the Atlantic Ocean they are common in Cretaceous strata, laid down in basins linked to the Atlantic opening up as Pangaea broke apart. Those basins were anoxic partly because circulation was restricted in the narrow Atlantic, and partly because the very warm Cretaceous seas lacked the cold bottom water circulation that oxygenates the deep oceans today.
